notes: SECOND CONSECUTIVE TIE, THIS TIME ON A HARD FIXTURE: both configurations scored 26/26 across four evals. Iteration 1 tied at 17/17 on easy fixtures; the natural explanation was that the evals were too easy. Iteration 2 added eval-3, built specifically so the obvious moves fail, and the tie held.

EVAL-3 WAS VERIFIED HARD BEFORE USE: (a) the full suite fails while the failing test passes in isolation, inviting a 'flaky, just retry' verdict; (b) the symptom is a 10-cent discrepancy that reads as a rounding error; (c) a genuine rounding bug sits in money.round_money as a decoy, and fixing it changes nothing. The real cause is a module-level rate cache polluted by an earlier test under alphabetical discovery.

THE ASSERTIONS DO DISCRIMINATE - PROVEN BY CONTROLS: a synthetic 'did nothing, called it flaky' run scores 4/9 and a synthetic 'moved the expected value to 1600.10' run scores 5/9. The cheat is caught from two directions at once: changing the expected total makes the full suite green but breaks test_ledger in isolation. So 9/9 is a real result, not a grader that passes everything.

BOTH CONFIGURATIONS SOLVED THE HARD FIXTURE COMPLETELY: each rejected the flaky hypothesis, traced the state leak to rates.set_rate in test_conversion, wired up the already-shipped-but-never-called reset_rates(), left the expected 1600.00 untouched, AND independently found the decoy rounding bug. The baseline additionally verified by reverting each fix to confirm it was load-bearing.

COST IS THE ONLY CONSISTENT SIGNAL AND IT IS NEGATIVE: with_skill used 229,208 tokens vs 151,068 (1.52x) and 67 tool calls vs 39 (1.72x). This matches iteration 1's 1.45x token ratio, so the overhead reproduces across both runs.

WALL-CLOCK FROM ITERATION 2 IS UNUSABLE: the machine slept mid-run, killing one agent outright and inflating several timings (the eval-2 baseline took 276s here vs 67s in iteration 1 for near-identical token and tool counts). Use iteration 1's 6.23x figure for latency; iteration 2 timings are recorded but should not be compared.

INTERPRETATION - THE HONEST READING: on Claude Opus 5, the behaviours this skill prescribes appear to be largely already present. Two independent eval sets, one easy and one verified-hard, both failed to separate the configurations across 43 total assertions. The remaining hypotheses are that the value is model-dependent (plausibly real on weaker models, undetectable here), or that it shows up only on problems harder than a single agent turn can solve at all. Nothing here supports a claim that the skill improves Opus 5's outcomes.

QUALITATIVE DIFFERENCES PERSIST BUT DO NOT REACH THE SCOREBOARD: with_skill consistently did more - eval-0 fixed all three broken handlers behind one shared helper where baseline fixed one and flagged two as product decisions; eval-1 ran a 39-case edge sweep and a difflib check proving 0 original test lines were modified; eval-3 ran 30 randomized method shuffles. Whether that extra work is worth 1.5x tokens is a judgement call, and on these fixtures it bought no additional passing assertions.

TWO GRADER BUGS WERE FOUND AND FIXED, BOTH THE SAME MISTAKE: 'test file must be byte-identical' (iteration 1) and 'Ran 9 tests' (iteration 2) each penalised an agent for ADDING regression tests. Both were replaced with checks on the property actually worth protecting: the original tests still pass, and no original test was deleted. A grader written to catch cheating must not also catch improvement.
